purpose: D2 — same workload as P3-B's overflow-scenario (named for parity; P3-C has no per-stream buffer/capacity to overflow), to observe how the reactive response/demand path behaves under the same slow-client condition.

client_observed.connection_result: completed normally, all 60 chunks delivered, no server-side rejection

finding: All 3.9MB delivered successfully — no application-level buffer overflow (there is no such buffer in this architecture). HEADLINE FINDING: terminal outcome=completed (and therefore admission-permit release) fired only 169ms after request start, while the client took 9.32s to actually finish receiving the data — a ~9.15s gap. This reflects WebFlux/Reactor Netty's demand-driven writing considering the response Flux 'complete' once all items are accepted into Reactor Netty's internal channel write buffer (gated by Netty writability/high-water-mark), not once bytes are confirmed delivered to the client. Postflight gauges are clean (0.0) but that clean state was reached at 169ms, not at the true 9.32s physical completion.
interpretation_constraints: Not a bug. Not a performance claim. Not evidence that P3-C is 'less safe' or P3-B is 'safer' — this is a measured architectural characteristic relevant to capacity planning (the admission ceiling bounds administratively-in-flight requests, not bytes still draining to slow clients in Reactor Netty's internal buffers). 'Reactive Streams backpressure exists' and 'the entire HTTP/WebClient/codec/OS stack is perfectly memory-bounded' are not the same claim.
